etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally a compound of 御(お) (o-, “honorific prefix”) + 父(とと) (toto, “father”) + 様(さま) (-sama, “honorific suffix”).
/ototosama/ → /otottsan/ → /otossan/
The /otossan/ → /otoosan/ progression was artificial; regular Japanese sound changes generally would not allow this shift. The /otoosan/ form first appears in the early Meiji period in educational materials mandated by the 文部省 (Monbushō, “Ministry of Education”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with 渇(かわ)く (kawaku, “to be thirsty”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 休(やす)む (yasumu, “to rest”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 動(どう)物(ぶつ) (dōbutsu, “animal”) + 園(えん) (-en, “garden”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The usage of the kanji 嘘 for うそ (uso, “lie”) can be considered as a kokuji (kokkun) because this character hasn't had the meaning of "lie" in Chinese at any time.
May originate as a semantic compound of 口 (“mouth”) and 虚 (“empty”), as in 虚(むな)しいことを口(くち)にする (munashii koto o kuchi ni suru, “to talk without any basis”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Attested in the late Heian period. Possibly cognate with 嘯(うそぶ)く (usobuku, “to boast”) and 似非(えせ) (ese, “fake, false”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From the Classical Japanese verb 増ゆ (fuyu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in 正倉院文書 (Shōsōin Monjo, “Shōsōin Documents”) with the spelling 宇利 (⟨uri⟩) (Omodaka 1967, p. 136). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *ur-.
Possibly cognate with Old Japanese 得 (u), modern Japanese 得る (eru, “to obtain, to get”), from the sense of getting money in exchange for the item sold.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/opoki/ → /oɸoki/ → /oɸoki na/ → /owoki na/ → /oːki na/
Appears starting from the Muromachi period (室(むろ)町(まち)時(じ)代(だい) (Muromachi jidai), c. 1336–1573).
Derived as the -na adjective construction of -i adjective 大(おお)きい (ōkii, “big, great”), which see for more.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/oːkina/ → /okːina/
Sound shift from ōkina. First attested in popular literature of the early 1800s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Chinese 大丈夫, equivalent to 大(だい) (dai-) + 丈(じょう)夫(ぶ) (jōbu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pansimara (“to begin”, intransitive).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
[pidari] → [ɸidari] → [çidari].
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *pintari.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 左 (MC tsaX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Possibly from 掴(つか)ま (tsukama, “to grab”, irrealis stem) + ふ (fu, frequentative suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with 優(やさ)しい (yasashii).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Likely from Middle Chinese compound 有名 (hjuw^X mjeng, literally “to have + name”). Compare modern Mandarin reading yǒumíng.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 服 (MC bjuwk).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sin-. Appears in the oldest Japanese texts, including the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE and the Man'yōshū of 759 CE.
The ぬ (-nu) ending historically had an irregular conjugation pattern, shared only by now-obsolete verb 往(い)ぬ, 去(い)ぬ (inu, “to go away, to go, to leave, to pass, to disappear”) and auxiliary verb ぬ (nu, indicating completion, generally reserved for non-intentional, spontaneous, or intransitive actions). The ぬ (-nu) in verb 死(し)ぬ (shinu) was viewed as identical to the auxiliary, and the verb 死(し)ぬ (shinu) initially was thus never conjugated with this auxiliary as an additional suffix.
The auxiliary itself may have derived from the verb 往(い)ぬ, 去(い)ぬ (inu, “to go away, to go, to leave, to pass, to disappear”), raising the possibility that the verb 死(し)ぬ (shinu) may have derived from a fusion of 死(し) (shi, “death”) + 往(い)ぬ, 去(い)ぬ (inu, “to go away, to go, to leave, to pass, to disappear”); the second element could also be the auxiliary ぬ (-nu) or its suggested ancient stative verb origin.
The transition from the ナ行(ぎょう)変(へん)格(かく)活(かつ)用(よう) (na-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “na-row irregular conjugation”) pattern to the regular 四(よ)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade conjugation”) appears in texts from the Muromachi period (1336–1573) and on. The na irregular pattern persisted in increasingly limited use until the Meiji period (1868–1929).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Derived as the intransitive form of Old Japanese verb 決(き)む (kimu, “to decide, to conclude; to be decided, to be concluded”).
The source verb kimu appears to follow a common pattern in Old Japanese verbs where the bare form is either transitive or intransitive, depending on context. This pattern persists in some modern verbs, such as つく (tsuku). Many of these Old Japanese verbs developed explicit transitive and intransitive forms, with one group adopting an -aru on the end for the intransitive (as the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis stem”) ending in -a + the conjugating る (ru) as the basic spontaneous or passive verb ending), and an -eru on the end for the transitive (as the 已(い)然(ぜん)形(けい) (izenkei, “realis or potential stem”) + the disappearing る (ru) as a generic verb ending).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Likely from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *oyonku. Included in The Tale of Genji from the late 900s or early 1000s. Listed in sources with a note that this may have been pronounced originally as oyoku, however, cognates among the Ryūkyūan languages would seem to support a voiced /ɡ/ as the final consonant. Compare Kunigami 泳じゅん (uijun), Okinawan 泳じゅん (qwiijun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the classical upper bigrade verb (カ行上二段活用) 生く.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese 痛し (itasi), from Proto-Japonic *ita (“painful”). Might originally be an interjection; compare English ouch.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨me₂⟩ → */məɨ/ → /me/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mai. Cognate with 目(ま) (ma, bound form). Now the modern Japanese term for eye.
Probably cognate with 見(み)る (miru, “to see, to look”).
May also be cognate with 芽(め) (me, “bud, shoot”), perhaps from the “visually prominent feature” sense, and with suppositional / volitional verb suffix む (mu) (presenting in modern Japanese verb conjugations as the -ō or -yō endings), perhaps from the “seem like, look like” sense.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 目 (MC mjuwk). Compare modern Cantonese 目 (muk₆) and Wu 目 (moq).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 目 (MC mjuwk). Compare modern Min Nan 目 (bo̍k).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, tentatively traced to Proto-Japonic *pasui (compare Ainu パスイ (pasui)). Probably related to 挟む (hasamu, “to pinch, to scissor, to hold between”), possibly also related to 嘴 (“beak”, pitch accent hàshí) or 端 (“tip”, pitch accent háꜜshì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 終(お)わる (owaru, “to end”, intransitive).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
* ⟨mi₁mi₁⟩ → */mimi/ → /mimi/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *mimi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ki₁ka yu⟩ → ⟨ki₁ko₂yu⟩ → */kʲikəju/ → /kikoju/ → /kikojeru/ → /kikoeru/
From Old Japanese verb 聞こゆ (kikoyu), itself derived from the 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of 聞く (kiku, “to hear, listen”) kika + ゆ (-yu, attributive suffix).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sisi. Not used in isolation in modern standard Japanese. Persists in compounds and in some dialects.
Cognate with 獣(しし) (shishi, “beast (especially one used for meat)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 肉 (MC nyuwk). Compare modern Hokkien 肉 (jio̍k / lio̍k), Teochew 肉 (ne̍k), or Hakka 肉 (ngiuk⁷).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Derived as the transitive/causative counterpart to intransitive verb 至る (itaru, “to come; to go; to reach a point in time or space; to result in”), originally meaning the same as causative conjugation 至らせる (itaraseru, “to make something or someone come or go; to make something reach a point in time or space; to cause a certain result”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨iro₂⟩ → */irə/ → /iro/
From Old Japanese.
First attested in the Nihon Shoki with the meaning of color. Senses referring to a person's emotions also appear quite early on. The romance or sex senses appear from the 900s, apparently an influence from Chinese usage, and roughly comparable to the euphemistic usage of English colorful.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨iro₂pe₂⟩ → */irəpəj/ → /irofe/ → /iroe/
Nominalization of the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of classical shimo nidan katsuyō verb 色う (irou, “to color something”).
Not used in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 色 (MC srik). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing.
The Buddhist sense is translation of Sanskrit रूप (rūpa, “outward appearance, color, form, shape”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 色 (MC srik). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tare/ → /dare/
From earlier tare.
The dare form appears from around the Edo period. The voicing of the initial /t-/ to /d-/ is likely by analogy with other interrogative demonstratives 何れ (dore, “which one”), 何処 (doko, “where”). See etymology 2
Now the primary form, replacing earlier tare.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki (712 CE) alongside its older form ta (see below).
Derived from older 誰 (ta, “who”) + れ (re, “thing”, demonstrative nominalizer ending). Compare the formation of これ (kore, “this”) from 此 (ko, “this”) + れ (re), 彼 (kare, “that one, that person”) from 彼 (ka, “that”) + れ (re), etc.
Superseded by dare above starting from around the Edo period. The tare form does not appear to be used anymore outside of poetry or intentionally archaic text.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki, completed roughly 712 CE.
Appears to be the oldest form.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
* ⟨wodo₂ru⟩ → */wodəru/ → /wodoru/ → /odoru/
From Old Japanese, with the original meaning of "to jump". First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *wontəru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the classical upper bigrade verb (ラ行上二段活用) 降(お)る (oru).
